ideas.title: Electricity took forty years to pay off
ideas.idea:
A new technology rarely pays off until people redesign the work around it, and that can take a generation.

By 1900 electric power had been on sale for two decades, yet American factories were barely more productive. Owners had swapped a big steam engine for a big electric motor and kept everything else: the overhead line shaft, the belts, the machines lined up wherever the shaft ran. Electricity's real gift was that every machine could have its own small motor, so a factory could be laid out around the flow of work instead of the route of the power. Lighter, single-storey, safer plants followed, but only as old mills wore out and managers learned to think differently. Productivity finally leapt in the 1920s.

The economist Paul David told this story in 1990 to explain why computers weren't yet showing up in the statistics.
why: Paul David (Stanford), 'The Dynamo and the Computer', American Economic Review, 1990: electric motors drove under 5% of US factory machinery in 1899 and just over half by the early 1920s; their spread accounts for about half the 1920s jump in manufacturing productivity growth.
Tim Harford (Financial Times) adds a human side: the gains also needed retrained workers with more responsibility, nudged by WWI-era limits on cheap labour.
Caveat: David himself warns the analogy is loose. Computers differ from dynamos, and a past lag doesn't predict a timetable for any technology today.

visual.label: How factories powered machines before electric motors — Core77
visual.note: Look at the photos of overhead shafts and belts: every machine had to sit under the shaft. That is the layout electricity eventually freed factories from. There's also a short clip of a working line-shaft shop.

ideas.title: Praise didn't make them worse
ideas.idea:
When something unusually good or bad happens, the next result will probably be closer to average, whatever you do. Daniel Kahneman learned this working with Israeli Air Force flight instructors. One insisted that praise backfired: cadets he praised for a superb manoeuvre usually flew worse next time, while those he shouted at improved. The pattern was real, but the cause was luck. An exceptional flight is partly skill and partly a good day, and good days don't repeat on demand, so the next attempt drifts back towards the cadet's normal level, praise or no praise.

The same trap catches the manager who 'fixes' a terrible quarter, the remedy taken at the worst point of a cold, and the club that sacks its coach after a losing run. Before crediting or blaming an intervention, ask whether things would have drifted back anyway.
why: Kahneman tells the story in Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), chapter 17.
Statisticians call it regression to the mean: wherever results mix skill with chance, extreme scores tend to be followed by less extreme ones. Francis Galton first described it in the 1880s.
Caveat: this doesn't mean feedback is useless. It means you need a comparison group, or many attempts, to tell whether it worked.

visual.label: Regression toward the mean — Wikipedia
visual.note: Look at Galton's height chart: children of very tall parents were tall, but less extreme than their parents.

ideas.title: The 'wood wide web' is mostly hype
ideas.idea: Trees probably aren't chatting through underground fungal networks, at least not the way bestsellers suggest. Mycorrhizal fungi are real and vital: they wrap tree roots, trading water and nutrients for sugar, and some link several trees at once. But in 2023 three forest ecologists led by Justine Karst at the University of Alberta reviewed the field evidence for three popular claims: that these networks are widespread in forests, that big trees feed seedlings through them, and that trees use them to send warnings. Each claim turned out to be thinly supported. Only two studies had actually mapped shared fungal links between trees, and seedlings connected to networks did no better on average. Meanwhile, citations overstating the original results had nearly doubled over 25 years. A good story had outrun its data.
why: Karst, Jones and Hoeksema, Nature Ecology & Evolution (2023), reviewed 26 seedling studies and more than 1,600 papers citing 18 key field studies.
The authors call the drift 'positive citation bias': each retelling slightly overstated what the original study showed.
Caveat: the fungi themselves are essential to forest health. The doubt is about network-wide sharing and signalling, not about mycorrhizae.

ideas.title: We overvalue what we build
ideas.idea:
Putting your own effort into making something makes you value it more, even when the result is mediocre. Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon and Dan Ariely called this the IKEA effect. Across four studies, people assembled IKEA storage boxes, folded origami and built Lego sets, then put a value on their work. They rated their amateur creations as similar in value to versions made by experts, and expected other people to agree. The extra love only appeared when the job was finished: when people built something and then had to take it apart, or never completed it, the effect faded.

It explains a lot at work: why teams defend their own designs, why 'not invented here' thinking is so stubborn, and why whoever built the spreadsheet struggles to see its flaws.
why: Norton, Mochon & Ariely, 'The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love', Journal of Consumer Psychology (2012).
The effect held for keen DIYers and complete novices alike, and depended on successfully completing the task.
Caveat: the items were cheap and simple, and the extra value lives mainly in the builder's eyes. A buyer won't share it.

ideas.title: Most of your fears never arrive
ideas.idea:
Much of what we dread hurts more in anticipation than it ever does in reality. Seneca made the point to his friend Lucilius nearly 2,000 years ago, writing that we "suffer more often in imagination than in reality". He offered a simple audit for any looming worry. Is it certain, or just rumour and suspicion? Is it truly harmful, or merely embarrassing? Is it happening now, or might it never come? Time, he noted, often intervenes: threats fade, get postponed or turn into something else. Meanwhile, the worrier has already paid in full.

This isn't advice to ignore risks. It's a way to separate a real problem you can act on today from a story your mind is running ahead of the facts.
why: Seneca, Letter 13 of the Moral Letters to Lucilius (around AD 65), quoted in Richard Gummere's 1917 translation.
Modern cognitive behavioural therapy uses a similar move, asking people to test anxious predictions against the evidence.
Caveat: some fears are accurate. The aim is to weigh them honestly, not to dismiss them.

ideas.title: Working complex systems start simple
ideas.idea:
If you want a complex system that works, start with a simple one that works and grow it. That's Gall's Law, from the paediatrician John Gall's 1975 book General Systemantics, a tongue-in-cheek study of why systems fail. His observation: every complex system that works turns out to have evolved from a simpler system that worked, while a complex system designed from scratch never works and can't be patched into working. You have to go back and start again with something simple.

Engineers recognise it in the internet, which grew from a four-computer network in 1969, and in the advice to build a minimum viable product first. It also explains why big-bang IT rollouts so often go wrong: too many untested interactions at once, and no working baseline to fall back to.
why: John Gall, General Systemantics (1975), later republished as Systemantics and The Systems Bible.
The same logic underpins iterative engineering: prototype, test, then add complexity one verified step at a time.
Caveat: it's a rule of thumb from experience, not a proven law. Some well-specified systems are designed whole and work, though usually from proven parts.

visual.note: Gall's other tongue-in-cheek rules are worth a skim, such as how fail-safe systems fail.

ideas.title: Hanoi's rat bounty bred more rats
ideas.idea:
Pay people per result and they'll find the cheapest way to produce that result, not the outcome you wanted. In 1902, French colonial officials in Hanoi were alarmed by rats swarming from the city's new sewers while plague spread across Asia. They offered a bounty of one cent per rat, and to spare officials from handling carcasses, a tail was enough proof. Soon tailless rats were spotted running through the streets: hunters were cutting off tails and releasing the animals to breed. Health inspectors later found rat farms on the city's outskirts, and the scheme was scrapped.

The historian Michael Vann, who found the story in French archives, points out it's better documented than the famous 'cobra effect'. The lesson: whenever you reward a measurable proxy, ask how someone could game it.
why: Michael G. Vann, 'Of Rats, Rice, and Race' (2003) and The Great Hanoi Rat Hunt (Oxford University Press, 2018).
Economists call this a perverse incentive, a close cousin of Goodhart's law: a measure stops being useful once it becomes a target.
Caveat: some details, such as how widespread the rat farms were, come from colonial reports and may be exaggerated.

visual.label: The Great Hanoi Rat Massacre of 1902 — Atlas Obscura

ideas.title: You have about 4,000 weeks
ideas.idea:
If you live to 80, you get just over 4,000 weeks. Oliver Burkeman built his 2021 book Four Thousand Weeks around that uncomfortable number, and his conclusion runs against most productivity advice: you will never get on top of everything, so stop trying. Becoming more efficient doesn't free you; it invites more tasks to fill the space, the way clearing your inbox earns you more email.

His alternative is to accept your limits and choose deliberately what to neglect. Decide which few things truly matter, do those first, and let the rest stay undone without guilt. Finitude isn't a problem for better time management to solve. It's what makes your choices mean something in the first place.
why: Oliver Burkeman, Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals (2021).
His 'efficiency trap' echoes the Jevons paradox: making something easier often means we end up doing more of it.
Caveat: the advice suits people with some control over their time. For many, the real constraint is workload, not mindset.

ideas.title: Study the planes that didn't return
ideas.idea:
The evidence in front of you has often been filtered by the very thing you're trying to understand. During the Second World War, the mathematician Abraham Wald, working with Columbia University's Statistical Research Group, studied damage on bombers that came back from missions. The tempting move was to add armour where the bullet holes clustered. Wald's insight was that the sample was missing the planes that never came back. Areas that looked clean on survivors were likely where hits were fatal, so that's where protection mattered most.

The same filter distorts everyday judgement: studying only successful founders, the old buildings still standing, or the customers who stayed. Before drawing a lesson from survivors, ask what the failures would have told you.
why: Wald wrote eight memoranda in 1943 on estimating aircraft vulnerability from returning planes; Mangel and Samaniego summarised them in the Journal of the American Statistical Association (1984).
The same reasoning applies wherever data has passed through a filter, from investment fund records to medical trials that lose drop-outs.
Caveat: the famous red-dotted plane picture is a later illustration, and some dramatic details of the popular story are embellished. The statistical point stands.

ideas.title: Spread-out study beats cramming
ideas.idea:
You'll remember far more if you split the same study time into sessions spread over days, rather than cramming it into one sitting. Hermann Ebbinghaus first measured this in the 1880s by memorising nonsense syllables and testing himself: memories faded fast, but each well-timed review flattened the forgetting curve. More than a century later, a 2006 review led by Nicholas Cepeda pooled 839 comparisons from 317 experiments and confirmed that spaced practice reliably beats massed practice. It also found a handy rule: the longer you need to remember something, the bigger the gaps between reviews should be.

Cramming feels productive because the material is fresh in the moment. That fluency is misleading. The effort of recalling something half-forgotten is what makes it stick.
why: Ebbinghaus, Memory (1885), mapped the forgetting curve using himself as the only subject.
Cepeda and colleagues, Psychological Bulletin (2006): the ideal gap between sessions grows with how long you need to retain the material.
Caveat: most studies use verbal recall, like vocabulary. Spacing seems to help complex skills too, but that evidence is thinner.

ideas.title: Efficiency can raise consumption
ideas.idea:
Making something more efficient can increase how much of it we use, not reduce it. In 1865, the economist William Stanley Jevons spotted a puzzle in Britain's coal figures. James Watt's improved steam engine burned far less coal for the same work, yet national coal consumption kept soaring. Cheaper power made steam worth using in mines, mills and factories that couldn't justify it before, so total demand grew faster than efficiency saved. Jevons concluded that using fuel economically does not mean using less of it.

Economists now call this the rebound effect. Fuel-efficient cars tempt people to drive further; cheaper computing gets spent on ever bigger models. Efficiency is still worth having, but if the aim is to use less, it usually needs a cap or a price signal alongside it.
why: William Stanley Jevons, The Coal Question (1865).
Later economists, including Khazzoom, Brookes and Saunders, extended the idea from single products to whole economies.
Caveat: full 'backfire', where total use actually rises, is debated. In most single markets the rebound is partial, so efficiency still cuts use.
